bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Liberty Global finishes taking itself apart and the market is forced to price the pieces instead of the conglomerate. At $9.59 (close, 27 July 2026) the whole company is worth about $3.27 billion on roughly 341 million shares. Against that, management's own raised year-end 2026 target for holding-company cash is about $2.0 billion, or roughly $5.86 a share, and the Liberty Growth portfolio of private investments carries an independently appraised value of $2.9 billion, or about $8.50 a share. Those two items alone come to roughly $14.36 a share. Buying the stock today therefore means paying about a third less than the cash and the investment portfolio are said to be worth, and receiving every operating telecom business for nothing. Chief executive Mike Fries made exactly that point on the 24 July 2026 call, noting the price then implied “essentially zero equity value attributed to our Liberty Telecom operations.”

The event meant to close that gap is the separation and Amsterdam listing of Ziggo Group, which combines VodafoneZiggo in the Netherlands with Telenet in Belgium into a single Benelux operator of roughly 13 million customers and about 6.6 billion euros (roughly $7.7 billion) of annual revenue. Liberty intends to distribute about 90% of it to its own shareholders, with Vodafone keeping 10%.

What makes this credible rather than promotional is that the sponsor has done it once already and the sub-milestones keep clearing. Liberty spun off Sunrise, its Swiss operator, in November 2024; management values that distributed stake at about $12 per Liberty Global share today, and it trades in Zurich at roughly 8 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. Since then: the Belgian regulator approved the Wyre-Proximus fiber-sharing agreement (cleared the day before the July call); every approval needed to buy Vodafone's half of the Dutch joint venture has been obtained, with closing due by the end of July 2026; new leadership for Ziggo Group was named and starts 1 September 2026; and management has raised about $1.2 billion this year, roughly $900 million from portfolio disposals plus a $340 million loan against the Wyre stake, which let it lift the year-end corporate cash target from about $1.5 billion to about $2.0 billion. On the strength of that progress Fries pulled the timing forward rather than pushing it back, saying the company is “a bit more ambitious on the timing of the spin off. And we are currently saying mid-2027 versus H2 2027.”

The private marks are also getting validated in cash rather than in slides. The company fully exited EdgeConneX in the second quarter for $604 million of proceeds, described as about four times the original investment over roughly ten years and better than a 30% annual return.

Underneath the event, the asset actually being separated is improving. VodafoneZiggo added 7,200 broadband customers in the quarter, its best result in more than six years, plus 31,700 postpaid mobile customers, with fixed revenue per user up 0.6%. Telenet added 6,100 broadband and 2,200 postpaid customers. If management delivers the stated equity story for Ziggo Group - leverage down to 4.5 times and free cash flow of 500 million euros by 2028 - and the market applies the free-cash-flow yield it already applies to Sunrise, Fries argues the listed Benelux group is worth up to $14 per Liberty Global share on its own.

Conditions that must hold: the Dutch stake purchase closes on schedule; the Belgian and Dutch asset sales of 1.2 to 1.4 billion euros execute and bring subsidiary debt down; the Benelux customer recovery continues rather than reverses; the private portfolio marks hold up as further positions are sold; and the board actually files and completes the listing rather than exercising its right to abandon it.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the discount is real, deserved, and self-perpetuating - and that nothing forces it to close for at least a year while the business underneath it shrinks.

Start with what actually broke. The board entry for this name carried a downside floor of $9.50. On 24 July 2026, the day second-quarter results landed, the stock traded as low as $9.30 intraday and closed at $9.60 on about 4.1 million shares, roughly five times its recent daily volume. The floor was breached within hours of the print and has not been recovered: the 27 July close was $9.59. It was never a floor; it was a recent price level, and the stated risk-to-reward of 4.7 to 1 was computed when the stock was near $11, which is where it traded when the results deck was written. The setup has moved materially against that entry.

The second-quarter numbers themselves were poor. Revenue of $1,172.0 million fell 7.7% as reported and 6.0% on a like-for-like basis. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of $324.9 million fell 3.1%. Adjusted free cash flow was negative $150.4 million, and the company posted a net loss of $357.8 million. Retained earnings have fallen from about $8.02 billion at September 2025 to about $5.08 billion at June 2026 - close to $3 billion of accumulated losses in three quarters. Consolidated net debt stands at about $6.66 billion.

The clearest problem is the asset that is not being separated. Virgin Media O2, the UK business Liberty owns half of alongside Telefonica, is deteriorating: revenue down 7.9% on a like-for-like basis, 28,200 broadband customers lost and 63,000 postpaid customers lost in the quarter, with full-year guidance for both revenue and earnings to decline 3% to 5% against capital spending of 2.0 to 2.2 billion pounds and adjusted free cash flow of only about 200 million pounds. Chief financial officer Charles Bracken conceded that “leverage is above our 4 to 5x target, and that credit spreads are currently elevated,” and on refinancing added “we acknowledge recent trading levels” - an admission the bonds have widened. A leveraged, shrinking half-stake can be worth zero, and in a bad enough outcome it can consume holding-company resources rather than contribute them.

Now attack the floor itself. The roughly $2.0 billion of corporate cash is not shareholder cash. It is the purchase price for Vodafone's half of the Dutch business. Fries said plainly the company will “end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view” - the asset sales funded the acquisition. That cash converts into an illiquid, leveraged telecom equity, and there is no dividend and no share repurchase creating a bid underneath the stock. The $2.9 billion investment portfolio is an appraisal, not a bid, with the top five positions accounting for more than half of it; concentrated private marks are exactly what gets cut when funding markets tighten. Haircut the portfolio by half and assign the operating telecoms nothing, and the honest floor is about $8.00 a share, roughly 17% below the current price rather than the 2% the board entry implied.

Finally, the event is soft and distant. There is no record date, no listing prospectus, no scheduled shareholder vote. The company's own words are “as early as mid-2027” - about eleven months away - the transaction still requires shareholder and exchange approvals, and the board explicitly retains discretion to abandon it. The headline value target also leans on 2028 assumptions: the $14-per-share figure for Ziggo Group requires free cash flow of 500 million euros, against combined guidance today of roughly 100 million euros at VodafoneZiggo and 20 million euros at Telenet. That is close to a fourfold increase in two years, and it is the weakest load-bearing number in the entire case.

What would confirm the bear: the mid-2027 language slipping back toward late 2027 or later; the Wyre stake sale missing its year-end 2026 to first-quarter 2027 window or clearing below the carrying mark; a writedown in the investment portfolio; further widening in Virgin Media O2 credit; or the Benelux customer recovery stalling before the listing.
sop_bull: Roughly $30 a share if the separation completes on the guided path and the market pays Sunrise-like multiples for the pieces. Built up on roughly 341 million shares: holding-company cash of about $2.0 billion, or $5.86 a share, taken at face value; the Liberty Growth private portfolio at its full independently appraised $2.9 billion, or $8.50 a share, which the EdgeConneX exit at about four times cost supports; Ziggo Group at management's stated ceiling of $14 a share, which requires the Benelux group to reach 500 million euros of free cash flow and 4.5 times leverage by 2028 and to be valued on the 10.5% to 13.5% free-cash-flow yield the market already applies to Sunrise; the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake recovering to about $1.50 a share as leverage comes down; and Virgin Media Ireland plus residual items at about $0.50. Note that the $12 a share of already-distributed Sunrise stock is deliberately excluded - shareholders hold it directly and it is not value inside these shares. Management's own “from an $18 stock we have a clear opportunity to create $37 to $40 of value” framing double-counts it; this figure does not.
sop_bear: About $8.00 a share, and this is the verified floor, not the board's $9.50. Built up on roughly 341 million shares: holding-company cash of about $2.0 billion, or $5.86 a share, using management's own raised year-end 2026 target and crediting it in full even though it is committed to the Vodafone purchase; the Liberty Growth portfolio haircut by half to about $1.45 billion, or $4.25 a share, on the grounds that appraisals are not bids and the top five positions are more than half the total; and the operating telecoms - the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake, Ziggo Group and Virgin Media Ireland - carried at zero, which is close to what the market pays for them today. That sums to about $10.11, from which roughly $2 a share is deducted for holding-company running costs, the risk that resources are drawn down to support a leveraged Virgin Media O2, and the discount the market persistently applies to a holding company that has not completed its break-up. For cross-reference, tangible book value - equity less goodwill and other intangibles - is about $13.32 a share and reported book value about $27.05, so the bear case is well inside accounting values. The severe case, in which the listing is abandoned and the portfolio is written down further, is closer to $6.50.
sop_breakdown:
Two numbers matter and they answer different questions. The sum of the parts, if the break-up completes and the value is recognised, is about $17.50 to $18.00 a share: holding-company cash $5.86, the Liberty Growth portfolio at a 25% haircut to its appraised mark $6.38, Ziggo Group at about half of management's $14 ceiling to reflect that the 500-million-euro free-cash-flow target is a 2028 number against roughly 120 million euros guided today $7.00, the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake $1.00, and Virgin Media Ireland plus residuals $0.50 - about $20.74 before applying a 15% discount for holding-company frictions and the eleven months of execution still required, giving roughly $17.60.

The base case actually used is lower, because the event is not certain. Weighting the event-resolved target of $18.00 at 60% and the verified downside floor of $8.00 at 40% gives about $14.00 a share. Against the 27 July close of $9.59 that is roughly 46% of expected upside. The 60% weighting reflects a sponsor that has completed this exact transaction before and has cleared every sub-milestone so far, offset by the absence of any binding date, filing or vote, and the board's retained right to walk away.
risk_reward: About 5.3 to 1 on corrected inputs, better than the 4.7 to 1 the board claimed but for a different reason than the board gave. From the 27 July 2026 close of $9.59, upside to the event-resolved target of $18.00 is about +88%; downside to the verified floor of $8.00 is about -17%. That is $8.41 of upside against $1.59 of downside. The board's stated ratio used a $9.50 floor and a price near $11 - and that floor was breached intraday at $9.30 on 24 July 2026 and has not been regained. So the ratio has improved only because the price fell through the advertised floor, not because the floor held. Measured against the probability-weighted base case of $14.00 rather than the target, the ratio is a more sober 2.8 to 1.
catalyst_summary: Ziggo Group, the combined Dutch and Belgian business, is set to be spun off and listed in Amsterdam “as early as mid-2027” - no record date, no filing, about eleven months out - offering roughly +88% to an $18 event-resolved value against about -17% to a verified $8.00 asset floor, with the stock at a 52-week low of $9.59 after the 24 July 2026 results.
dated_milestone:
Verified on 28 July 2026 against the second-quarter results released 24 July 2026, the investor call of the same date, and the 1 June 2026 leadership announcement; no new disclosure has landed since the 24 July current report and quarterly report, so the status below is current.

No binding date exists for the event itself. The firm dates that do exist are preparatory: closing of the purchase of Vodafone's 50% interest in VodafoneZiggo by 31 July 2026, with all approvals already obtained; the new Ziggo Group chief executive and chief financial officer taking office on 1 September 2026, with the balance of the leadership team to be announced in September 2026; the sale of a stake in Wyre targeted for year-end 2026 or the first quarter of 2027; and 1.2 to 1.4 billion euros of Belgian and Dutch asset sales under way to reduce subsidiary debt. The listing itself is guided only as “as early as mid-2027”, accelerated from a prior “second half of 2027”, and remains subject to shareholder and exchange approval with the board retaining the right to abandon it.
forcing_function:
There is no single hard date that forces a re-rating, and that is the central weakness of this setup. The genuine trigger is the filing of a listing prospectus for Ziggo Group together with a scheduled shareholder vote, because that is the moment the separation stops being a plan and becomes a transaction with a calendar. That filing has not happened and has not been scheduled.

Before it, four checkpoints will move the odds. First, closing the purchase of Vodafone's half of the Dutch business by 31 July 2026 - imminent, fully approved, and foundational, because Ziggo Group cannot be formed without it. Second, the September 2026 completion of the Ziggo Group management team, which converts an intention into an operating company with its own leadership and reporting line. Third, the sale of the Wyre stake, targeted for year-end 2026 or the first quarter of 2027, which both tests the private marks in cash and funds the Belgian deleveraging the equity story depends on. Fourth, third-quarter results in late October 2026, the next occasion on which the mid-2027 language will either be reaffirmed or quietly stretched.

There is also a mechanical flow event further out. Because the shares to be distributed will list on Euronext Amsterdam rather than in the United States, index funds and mandates that cannot hold a foreign listing will be forced to sell the distributed stock. That is the classic post-separation supply that tends to create a better entry in the spun business than in the parent - a reason to expect the value to be recognised after the listing rather than on the day it happens.
consensus_delta:
The market is treating Liberty Global as a leveraged European cable operator and valuing it off consolidated, declining earnings - revenue down 7.7% in the second quarter, adjusted free cash flow of negative $150.4 million, a net loss of $357.8 million. On that lens the stock looks like a melting ice cube and $9.59 looks generous.

What that lens misses is that the consolidated figures include businesses being actively dismantled while excluding where the value sits. Holding-company cash at the raised year-end 2026 target of about $2.0 billion is $5.86 a share. The independently appraised Liberty Growth portfolio at $2.9 billion is $8.50 a share. Together that is roughly $14.36 against a $9.59 stock - a 33% discount to cash and investments alone, with every operating telecom business thrown in free. That is not a soft claim: management raised the cash target from $1.5 billion after beating its own disposal plan by a wide margin, banking about $1.2 billion year to date, and it realised EdgeConneX in the quarter for $604 million at roughly four times cost and better than a 30% annual return. The street is marking a portfolio to scepticism that has just been marked to cash at a premium.

The second thing the street has wrong is direction of travel on the event. The consensus reflex on any European telecom break-up is that it slips. This one was pulled forward: mid-2027 from the second half of 2027, on the back of a Belgian regulatory approval, full approval to buy out Vodafone's Dutch stake, and named leadership.

But there is a bull-side consensus error too, and honesty requires naming it. Published bullish work has run base cases as high as $27 a share by treating the holding-company cash as shareholder value and the appraised portfolio at face. It is neither free nor liquid: the cash is the purchase price for the Vodafone stake and converts into an illiquid leveraged equity, and the portfolio is five big private positions carried at appraisal. The market's discount is not irrational - it is a reasonable haircut for concentration, illiquidity, and a half-stake in a UK operator whose bonds have widened and whose leverage management admits sits above target. The genuine disagreement is narrower than the bulls claim: roughly $18 of parts value, not $27.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are the hard part, because every source of support is switched off while the trigger is still a year away.

Cash generation is negative right now. Adjusted free cash flow was negative $150.4 million in the second quarter and the company posted a $357.8 million net loss, on top of roughly $3 billion of accumulated losses since September 2025. Consolidated net debt is about $6.66 billion.

The holding-company cash cannot help the share price. It is earmarked for the Vodafone purchase closing by 31 July 2026 - Fries said the company will “end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view” - and there is no dividend and no share repurchase. Nothing bids for the stock on weakness, which is precisely why it cut through the $9.50 level on the print without pausing and has stayed below it since.

The sharpest near-term risk is Virgin Media O2. Revenue fell 7.9% on a like-for-like basis; the business lost 28,200 broadband and 63,000 postpaid customers in the quarter; guidance is for revenue and earnings both to decline 3% to 5% while capital spending runs at 2.0 to 2.2 billion pounds, leaving adjusted free cash flow of about 200 million pounds. Management acknowledged leverage above the 4 to 5 times target, elevated credit spreads, and unfavourable trading levels on its bonds. If UK credit widens further, the market will start pricing the possibility that the parent has to support it - which attacks the cash floor directly.

There is also execution risk in the Belgian restructuring itself. Wyre is drawing a large underwritten facility to repay a roughly $2.3 billion intercompany loan to Telenet and pay a $400 million dividend, with Telenet then retiring 2028 maturities. That plumbing has to work, in a market where the company itself says spreads are elevated.

Finally, the calendar. Third-quarter results in late October 2026 are the next opportunity for the mid-2027 language to be stretched. Any softening there, or a Wyre stake sale that misses its window or clears below the carrying mark, would take the stock toward the $8.00 floor well before any listing document exists.
positioning_washout:
The forced selling has partly already happened, and the more interesting wave is still ahead.

This shareholder base is not yield-driven - there is no dividend to cut - so the classic income-fund exodus does not apply. It is a value and event-driven register, and that register capitulated on the results. The stock traded to $9.30 intraday on 24 July 2026 on about 4.1 million shares, roughly five times its recent daily volume, closing at $9.60 and setting a 52-week low against a $13.12 high in February. It closed 27 July at $9.59 on continued heavy turnover of about 4.5 million shares across the share classes, so the break has been held rather than reversed. That is what exhaustion looks like: a heavy break of a widely watched level, then a market that will not bid it back. One secondary source reported an unusual spike in put buying on the A shares around the print - roughly 33,000 contracts against a typical 714 a day - which, if accurate, points to hedging or bearish positioning immediately after the results rather than accumulation. That is a single low-quality source and should be treated as colour, not evidence.

The absence of a company bid matters more than usual. With repurchases off while cash funds the Vodafone purchase, there is no price-insensitive buyer to absorb tax-loss selling into year-end 2026, and this stock is sitting on losses for anyone who bought above $11.

The larger mechanical event comes at the separation itself. Liberty holders will receive shares in a company listed on Euronext Amsterdam, not in the United States. Index funds tracking US benchmarks, and mandates barred from holding foreign-listed securities, will have to sell the distributed stock regardless of value. That indiscriminate supply is the well-worn reason spun-off companies are often cheapest in the weeks after listing. For this thesis it cuts two ways: it argues the value gets recognised after the listing rather than at it, and it argues the better entry may eventually be in Ziggo Group itself rather than in the parent today.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good ratio attached to a slow, soft trigger, and it arrives after the advertised safety net has already given way. Both halves of that sentence need to be held at once.

What is genuinely strong: the sponsor. Liberty Global has completed this exact manoeuvre before - Sunrise, spun in November 2024, is worth roughly $12 per Liberty share to holders who received it - and every checkable sub-milestone for the second one has cleared. Belgian regulatory approval is in hand, all approvals to buy Vodafone's half of the Dutch business are obtained with closing due by 31 July 2026, leadership is named for 1 September 2026, about $1.2 billion has been raised against plan, and the year-end cash target was raised rather than cut. Management pulled the timing forward, to mid-2027 from the second half of 2027. Meanwhile the asset being separated is improving: VodafoneZiggo posted its best broadband quarter in more than six years. The valuation gap is real and arithmetic, not rhetorical - about $14.36 a share of cash and appraised investments against a $9.59 stock, with the operating telecoms free.

What disqualifies it from size today: the event is not dated. “As early as mid-2027” is roughly eleven months away, with no record date, no listing prospectus, no scheduled vote, and an explicit board right to abandon. That is a plan, not a scheduled event, and nothing forces the market's hand in the meantime. Worse for the entry premise, the $9.50 downside floor this name was admitted on did not survive its first test - the stock traded through it to $9.30 on 24 July 2026 and has closed below it every session since, at a 52-week low. Rebuilding the floor honestly from the balance sheet puts it near $8.00: holding-company cash of $5.86 a share, which is committed to an acquisition rather than distributable, plus the private portfolio at a 50% haircut, with the telecoms at zero. A real floor exists. It just sits about 17% lower than the one that was underwritten.

And the interim is genuinely unpleasant. Free cash flow is negative, there is no buyback and no dividend to support the shares, and the half-owned UK operator is losing broadband and mobile customers with leverage above target and credit spreads management concedes are elevated.

So: wait, with named conditions rather than a vague hope of a flush. Three things would change this from a watch to a purchase. First, a Ziggo Group listing prospectus filed or a shareholder vote scheduled - the moment the event acquires a calendar. Second, the Wyre stake sale completing at or above its carrying value in the year-end 2026 to first-quarter 2027 window, which would test the private marks in cash for a second time after EdgeConneX. Third, price: the balance-sheet floor is near $8.00, and a wash toward $8.50 would offer a genuine margin of safety rather than the notional one this name was entered on. Conversely, if the October 2026 results stretch the mid-2027 language, the thesis weakens rather than merely waits.

The value case underneath is sound - a verifiable discount to cash and investments, run by a team that has delivered a separation before - and the odds have improved slightly as the price fell while the parts did not. It simply does not need to be owned this month, and the discipline of this funnel is that an undated event eleven months out, entered below a floor that has already broken, does not earn real capital.
interrogator_dossier:
# Liberty Global (LBTYK) — Event Dossier

**Event under examination:** the planned separation and Euronext Amsterdam listing of "Ziggo Group", the newly formed Benelux telecom company combining VodafoneZiggo in the Netherlands with Telenet in Belgium.
**Prepared:** 28 July 2026. **Live price:** $9.59 (close, 27 July 2026; the A shares closed at $9.83). **Market value:** about $3.27 billion on roughly 341 million shares.
**Re-verification:** checked again on 28 July 2026. Nothing new has been disclosed since the second-quarter results — the company's most recent filings remain the current report and quarterly report both dated 24 July 2026. The event status below is unchanged, and the share price has slipped a further eleven cents to a fresh low.

---

## 0. THE HEADLINE FINDING

Two things are true at once here, and the board entry for this name captures neither cleanly.

First, the sponsor is credible and the plan is moving forward, not backward. On the 24 July 2026 second-quarter call, chief executive Mike Fries said the company is "a bit more ambitious on the timing of the spin off. And we are currently saying mid-2027 versus H2 2027." That is an acceleration. Most soft catalysts in this funnel slip; this one was pulled forward, and it was pulled forward because real, checkable building blocks were completed.

Second, the event is still not a dated, binding one. There is no record date, no listing prospectus, no shareholder vote scheduled. The company's own language is "as early as mid-2027" — roughly eleven months away — and the board retains the discretion to abandon the transaction. An eleven-month soft target is a plan, not a hard, scheduled event.

The more damaging finding concerns the downside floor. The board entry carries a floor of $9.50. On 24 July 2026, the day of the second-quarter results, the stock traded as low as $9.30 intraday and closed at $9.60. The floor has already been breached, and the stock has not recovered it — the 27 July close of $9.59 is below it again. It was not a floor; it was a recent price. The board's stated risk-to-reward of 4.7 to 1 was struck when the stock was near $11, which is where it was trading when the results deck was written. The setup has moved against the entry since.

That said, when I rebuild the floor from the balance sheet rather than from the chart, a real one does exist — it just sits lower, around $8.00. On corrected inputs the asymmetry is intact and slightly better than a week ago, because the price fell while the parts did not. The problem with this name today is not the ratio. It is that the event is undated and far away, the near-term cash generation is negative, and the advertised safety margin was overstated.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC — what management is actually doing

Liberty Global is deliberately taking itself apart. This is not a compounding story and management does not pretend otherwise.

The template was set in November 2024, when the company spun off Sunrise, its Swiss operator, to shareholders. Fries now values that distributed stake at about $12 per Liberty Global share, noting Sunrise trades in Zurich at roughly 8 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, or a 10.5% to 13.5% free-cash-flow yield (free cash flow divided by market value). Importantly, that $12 sits in shareholders' hands already — it is not value still inside the shares being analysed here, and any thesis that counts it twice is wrong.

Ziggo Group is the second act. It combines the Dutch and Belgian operations into a single Benelux group of roughly 13 million customers and €6.6 billion (about $7.7 billion) of annual revenue. The structure is a hybrid: Liberty Global intends to distribute about 90% of the shares to its own shareholders, with Vodafone retaining 10% following Liberty's purchase of Vodafone's half of the Dutch joint venture.

Alongside that, the company has been converting its private investment portfolio — "Liberty Growth" — into cash. Fries described the strategy plainly: "despite the size and scale and growth prospects of our businesses, we believe our stock today reflects no value for these assets."

**Read:** the narrative has been consistent and it is being executed against, not merely narrated. That is unusual and it counts.

## 2. CLAIMS vs EVIDENCE (forensic)

Where the story is poorer than the numbers: the second quarter itself was soft. ## 3. THE OPERATING BUSINESSES — where the risk actually sits

The Benelux assets going into the spin are stabilising. This is the honest reason the shares are at a 52-week low. The market is not disputing the Benelux plan; it is marking the UK stake toward zero and questioning whether it stays there.

---

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — rebuilt from the balance sheet

Liberty Global is deliberately taking itself apart. This is not a compounding story and management does not pretend otherwise.

Ziggo Group is the second act. It combines the Dutch and Belgian operations into a single Benelux group of roughly 13 million customers and €6.6 billion (about $7.7 billion) of annual revenue. The Benelux assets going into the spin are stabilising. This is the honest reason the shares are at a 52-week low. The market is not disputing the Benelux plan; it is marking the UK stake toward zero and questioning whether it stays there.

The board entry's $9.50 floor does not survive contact with the tape. Here is what does, per share on roughly 341 million shares:

Fries said the company will "end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view" — the asset sales funded the acquisition of Vodafone's stake. - **Liberty Growth portfolio** at the appraised $2.9 billion: **$8.50**, with the top five holdings more than half the total. At a 50% haircut for the fact that appraisals are not bids: **$4.25**.

---

High, with one caveat. This management team has completed a separation of exactly this type before, and the result was good — Sunrise is worth roughly $12 per Liberty Global share to holders who received it. They have beaten their own cash-raising plan this year rather than missed it. They obtained every approval needed for the Dutch stake purchase. They named the incoming leadership. They pulled the timing forward rather than pushing it back. And they told shareholders that internal estimates of the synergies now exceed the $1 billion of net present value previously announced, while declining to publish the higher number — restraint rather than promotion.

Read the parts, not the headline.

---

The asymmetry is genuinely attractive and the sponsor is genuinely credible. But the event is roughly eleven months away, carries no record date and no filing, and can be abandoned at the board's discretion — while the company burns cash, the UK stake deteriorates, and no repurchase supports the shares. Nothing forces the market's hand before a listing prospectus exists.

The single most important thing to weigh: **this is a good ratio attached to a slow, soft trigger, entered after the advertised floor already gave way.** The correct response to that is patience with named conditions, not size.

A real, well-progressed, company-guided separation with credible sub-milestones already cleared — but no fixed date, no filing, no binding obligation, and a target window that begins about eleven months out. - **The live catalyst (the load-bearing event):** Liberty Global is creating "Ziggo Group," combining its Belgian operator Telenet with its Dutch joint venture VodafoneZiggo into a single Benelux business serving about 13 million customers with roughly €6.6 billion in annual revenue.   2. Liberty Global then plans to list Ziggo Group locally on Euronext Amsterdam and spin off the 90% it will hold to its own shareholders in the second half of 2027.
